newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says Bonn will not accept EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Bonn will not accept EMU delay.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday for the first time categorically ruled out a delay in launching European monetary union in 1999, reaffirming that Germany would meet all the entry criteria.
"Germany will never accept a delay in the timetable," he said. "Under no circumstances."
"Germany will completely fulfil the criteria," he added in remarks to industrialists in Duesseldorf.

Kohl's comments came as two leading German economists argued that a delay should be seen as a possibility, saying it made little sense to stick rigidly to a timetable if the fundamental basis for a stable currency was not there.

Reimut Jochimsen, a member of the central bank's council, said he did not support talk of delaying the EMU project to create the single currency, to be called the euro, but a delay should not be completely ruled out.

In the text of a speech delivered in Luxembourg and made available here in advance, Jochimsen argued that economic and monetary union could start on time in January 1999 only if a small group of qualified countries took part.

"If the deadline set out in the treaty is to be kept, but if on the other hand there is to be no decision at the euro's expense, it follows that only a start with a small circle of really qualified countries can be considered," Jochimsen said.
The criteria should not be softened and all candidates taking part in monetary union should be judged on the same measure, not by a politically-motivated "gentlemen's agreement," he added.
A much stronger case for delay was argued by Juergen Donges, one of a panel of economic advisers known as the "five wise men."
Donges told Reuters that he saw no real chance for Germany to meet the fiscal entry criteria, adding that this was the case both on the budget and on the debt assessments.

He said that if monetary union could not begin with a large enough group of countries, then it would be better to delay the start. It was more important to ensure that the criteria were met adequately than to start on time, he said.
"History will measure monetary union on the criteria of whether it really produces a stable currency and not on the basis of whether it began on a certain day," he said.
Countries that wish to enter monetary union in 1999 must meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, total debt and public deficits this year.

For most countries, the requirement calling for a deficit equal to no more than 3 percent of gross domestic product is proving the hardest to meet. Germany is aiming for a 2.9 percent level this year, which many see as optimistic.
On public debt, the ideal target is 60 percent of GDP. Countries with much higher debt levels must at least show that they are making progress toward that level.

Germany is currently running a debt level of just over 60 percent, which is set to rise this year, but has already pleaded that the special situation of German unification should warrant it special treatment in the final assessment.
The European Commission forecast Wednesday that Germany would hit the deficit target on the head, with a 3.0 percent this year.
But Germany's six major economic institutes were more sceptical, forecasting 3.0 to 3.2 percent.
The institutes said, however, that they believed monetary union should go ahead on time even if Germany overshot this one target by a relatively small margin.
